title.rendered: Cannabis in Wellness Tourism: Emerging Trends for 2025

content.rendered:
The convergence of cannabis and wellness tourism is reshaping travel experiences worldwide. As cannabis becomes more widely accepted and legalized, wellness retreats, spas, and destinations are incorporating it into their offerings, creating a lucrative and innovative market segment. In 2025, cannabis wellness tourism is set to thrive, blending relaxation, healing, and exploration in unique ways.

The Rise of Cannabis Wellness Tourism

The rise of cannabis-infused wellness experiences can be attributed to several factors:

  • Legalization Momentum: As more countries and states legalize cannabis, travelers are seeking destinations where they can safely and legally incorporate it into their wellness routines.
  • Health and Well-Being Focus: Modern travelers prioritize mental and physical well-being, and cannabis’ therapeutic properties align with this growing trend.
  • Experiential Travel: Consumers are increasingly drawn to unique and memorable travel experiences, and cannabis wellness tourism provides a fresh perspective on relaxation and self-care.

Popular Cannabis Wellness Experiences

Cannabis wellness tourism offers a variety of experiences tailored to different preferences and needs:

  • Cannabis-Infused Spas: Luxury spas are introducing cannabis-infused treatments, including massages, facials, and body wraps that utilize CBD or THC products to promote relaxation and pain relief.
  • Wellness Retreats: Retreats combining yoga, meditation, and cannabis consumption create holistic experiences that foster relaxation, creativity, and mindfulness.
  • Culinary Experiences: Cannabis-infused dining experiences and cooking classes allow travelers to explore the culinary potential of cannabis while learning about its health benefits.
  • Nature Immersion: Destinations offering guided cannabis-friendly hikes, forest bathing, or glamping experiences provide a deeper connection to nature.

Destinations Leading the Way

Several regions are emerging as leaders in cannabis wellness tourism:

  • California, USA: Known for its progressive cannabis laws, California hosts a variety of wellness retreats and cannabis-friendly accommodations.
  • Canada: With nationwide legalization, Canada offers cannabis-infused spa treatments, retreats, and tours across its provinces.
  • Jamaica: Renowned for its cultural ties to cannabis, Jamaica’s wellness tourism scene blends traditional practices with modern cannabis experiences.
  • Thailand: With recent legalization, Thailand is exploring cannabis-infused wellness treatments in its globally recognized spa industry.

Challenges and Opportunities

While the potential for cannabis wellness tourism is immense, challenges remain:

  • Regulatory Complexities: Variations in cannabis laws across regions create challenges for travelers and businesses.
  • Education and Stigma: Destigmatizing cannabis use and educating consumers about its benefits are critical to mainstreaming cannabis wellness tourism.
  • Standardization and Safety: Ensuring the quality and consistency of cannabis products used in wellness treatments is vital for consumer trust.

Future Trends in Cannabis Wellness Tourism

The future of cannabis wellness tourism will likely include:

  • Personalized Experiences: Integration of AI and health data to create customized wellness programs tailored to individual needs.
  • Cannabis and Traditional Medicine: Blending cannabis with traditional healing practices like Ayurveda and acupuncture to offer holistic therapies.
  • Sustainability Focus: Eco-friendly cannabis tourism initiatives, such as sustainable farming and carbon-neutral retreats, will appeal to environmentally conscious travelers.
  • Cross-Industry Collaboration: Partnerships between cannabis companies, wellness brands, and travel agencies to create comprehensive wellness travel packages.

Conclusion

Cannabis wellness tourism is more than a niche trend; it’s a transformative movement redefining the boundaries of relaxation and self-care. By integrating cannabis into wellness experiences, the travel industry is opening doors to innovative and inclusive journeys that cater to the evolving preferences of modern travelers. As legalization spreads and consumer interest grows, 2025 is set to be a landmark year for this burgeoning sector.

title.rendered: Sustainability in Cannabis Packaging: The Green Revolution

content.rendered:
As the cannabis industry continues its rapid growth, the environmental impact of packaging has become a pressing concern. In 2025, sustainability is no longer an optional trend but a necessity for cannabis companies aiming to meet consumer expectations and regulatory demands. With innovative materials, design strategies, and circular economy models, the industry is embracing a green revolution in packaging.

The Environmental Challenge of Cannabis Packaging

The cannabis industry generates significant packaging waste due to stringent regulations requiring child-resistant, tamper-proof, and often single-use materials. Common challenges include:

  • Excessive Plastic Use: Many cannabis products are packaged in single-use plastics, contributing to the global plastic pollution crisis.
  • Regulatory Overlap: State and national packaging laws often conflict, making it difficult for companies to adopt standardized sustainable practices.
  • Consumer Perception: While eco-consciousness is growing, many consumers remain unaware of the environmental footprint of cannabis packaging.

Innovations in Sustainable Packaging

To address these challenges, cannabis companies are adopting innovative solutions that prioritize both functionality and sustainability:

  • Biodegradable Materials: Packaging made from hemp, corn-based bioplastics, or mycelium (mushroom roots) offers compostable alternatives to traditional plastics.
  • Recyclable Packaging: Brands are designing packaging that can be easily separated and recycled, reducing contamination in recycling streams.
  • Reusable Containers: Some companies are introducing deposit-return systems for glass jars and tins, encouraging consumers to return packaging for reuse.
  • Minimalist Design: By reducing the size and complexity of packaging, businesses are cutting down on material use and production waste.

Case Studies: Leaders in Sustainable Cannabis Packaging

Several companies are leading the way in sustainable packaging:

  • Sun Grown Packaging: Known for their fully recyclable, child-resistant paperboard packaging, Sun Grown offers a viable alternative to plastic-heavy designs.
  • Sana Packaging: This innovative company creates packaging from reclaimed ocean plastic and domestically grown industrial hemp.
  • PAX Labs: PAX’s reusable vape pods and streamlined designs reduce waste while maintaining product quality.

The Role of Technology

Advancements in technology are enabling more sustainable packaging solutions:

  • Smart Packaging: QR codes and RFID tags embedded in packaging provide product information digitally, reducing the need for printed materials.
  • AI-Driven Design: Machine learning algorithms optimize packaging designs to use fewer materials without compromising safety or functionality.
  • Blockchain for Transparency: Blockchain technology ensures traceability, verifying that packaging materials are sourced sustainably.

Consumer and Regulatory Shifts

The push for sustainable cannabis packaging is driven by both consumer demand and evolving regulations:

  • Eco-Conscious Consumers: Millennials and Gen Z, who make up a significant portion of the cannabis market, are prioritizing environmentally friendly brands.
  • Government Incentives: Regulatory bodies are introducing incentives for companies that adopt sustainable practices, including tax breaks and certification programs.
  • Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR): Laws mandating that companies bear the cost of recycling their packaging are gaining traction globally.

Looking Ahead: The Circular Economy in Cannabis

The ultimate goal for sustainable packaging is a circular economy, where waste is minimized, and materials are continually reused. Key components include:

  • Closed-Loop Systems: Collaborations between brands, retailers, and recyclers to ensure packaging returns to the production cycle.
  • Consumer Education: Informing consumers about how to properly dispose of or return cannabis packaging is crucial for the success of sustainable initiatives.
  • Standardization: Industry-wide standards for sustainable packaging materials and practices can streamline adoption and reduce costs.

Conclusion

Sustainability in cannabis packaging is not just a responsibility—it’s an opportunity to innovate and lead. Companies that prioritize eco-friendly solutions will not only meet regulatory requirements but also build trust and loyalty with consumers. As the cannabis industry grows, the green revolution in packaging offers a pathway to a more sustainable and prosperous future for all.

title.rendered: AI and Cannabis: How Machine Learning is Transforming Consumer Experiences in 2025

content.rendered:
As technology continues to intersect with the cannabis industry, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are becoming central to how businesses and consumers navigate this rapidly evolving market. From personalized recommendations to optimizing retail operations, AI is reshaping the cannabis consumer experience in unprecedented ways. Here’s a closer look at the key innovations and trends defining AI’s role in the cannabis space in 2025.

Personalized Cannabis Recommendations

One of the most transformative applications of AI is in helping consumers find the right cannabis products for their needs. With thousands of strains, edibles, and concentrates available, choice can be overwhelming. AI is making this process seamless through:

  • Tailored Suggestions: Platforms like PotBotics use AI-driven algorithms to analyze a consumer’s preferences, medical history, and desired effects, recommending products that align with their unique profiles.
  • Symptom-Based Matching: By integrating with health apps, AI systems can suggest cannabis products based on specific symptoms, such as anxiety, pain, or insomnia, backed by lab data and user feedback.
  • Dynamic Learning: AI tools learn and evolve based on consumer behavior, ensuring that recommendations improve over time.

Enhancing Retail Experiences

In cannabis dispensaries and online stores, AI is revolutionizing how products are presented and sold:

  • Smart Budtenders: AI-powered kiosks and virtual assistants provide instant answers to customer questions, helping them make informed decisions without relying solely on human staff.
  • Inventory Management: Machine learning algorithms analyze sales trends to predict inventory needs, ensuring dispensaries remain stocked with popular products while minimizing waste.
  • Consumer Analytics: AI tools gather data on buying patterns to help businesses tailor marketing strategies and promotions to specific customer segments.

Improving Product Quality and Safety

AI is also playing a critical role in ensuring the quality and safety of cannabis products:

  • Lab Testing Automation: Machine learning models streamline the analysis of cannabinoids, terpenes, and contaminants, ensuring products meet stringent safety standards.
  • Predictive Cultivation: AI systems monitor environmental conditions in real time, optimizing growing processes to produce consistent, high-quality crops.
  • Counterfeit Detection: Blockchain and AI integration help track product origins, ensuring authenticity and reducing the risk of counterfeit goods in the market.

Challenges in AI Integration

While the potential of AI in cannabis is vast, there are hurdles to overcome:

  • Data Privacy: As AI systems collect consumer and operational data, ensuring privacy and compliance with regulations is paramount.
  • Cost Barriers: Implementing AI technology can be expensive, posing challenges for smaller businesses.
  • Regulatory Complexity: Navigating the patchwork of cannabis laws complicates the deployment of standardized AI solutions.

Future Trends to Watch

The role of AI in cannabis is only set to grow. Some trends to watch in 2025 include:

  • Voice-Activated Shopping: Integration with smart devices could allow consumers to order cannabis products via voice commands.
  • AI-Powered Wellness Plans: Comprehensive health platforms may use AI to integrate cannabis recommendations with overall wellness regimens, combining exercise, diet, and mental health strategies.
  • Global Standardization: As cannabis becomes more widely accepted, AI could help create global standards for product labeling, quality control, and consumer safety.

Conclusion

In 2025, AI is more than just a buzzword in the cannabis industry—it’s a driving force behind better consumer experiences, improved product quality, and smarter business operations. As technology and cannabis continue to evolve together, the integration of AI promises a future where personalization, efficiency, and safety define the market. For businesses and consumers alike, these innovations are paving the way for a more accessible and enjoyable cannabis journey.

title.rendered: Growing Selection of Hemp Products: Pioneering Sustainability in 2025

content.rendered:
Hemp, one of nature’s most versatile plants, is at the heart of a sustainability revolution. As we enter 2025, the hemp industry is thriving, offering an ever-expanding array of products that cater to eco-conscious consumers and industries alike. From textiles to food to innovative materials, hemp is proving to be a key player in reducing environmental impact while meeting modern demands.

Why Hemp Is the Ultimate Sustainable Crop

Hemp’s resurgence as a favored crop is not just a trend but a necessity. Its unique properties make it a sustainable choice for various industries:

  • Low Resource Use: Hemp requires significantly less water than conventional crops and can thrive without pesticides, making it an environmentally friendly choice.
  • Soil Health: Hemp regenerates soil by removing toxins and adding nutrients, making it a preferred crop for sustainable farming practices.
  • Carbon Sequestration: As it grows, hemp absorbs large amounts of CO2, contributing to its status as a carbon-negative crop.
  • Rapid Growth: Hemp grows quickly, allowing for multiple harvests per year in suitable climates, increasing its economic and ecological benefits.

Innovative Hemp-Based Products in 2025

The versatility of hemp has led to its incorporation into a growing list of products. Some of the most exciting developments include:

  • Hempcrete: This eco-friendly building material is gaining traction in the construction industry for its insulating properties and ability to sequester carbon.
  • Bioplastics: Hemp-based plastics are offering a sustainable alternative to traditional petroleum-based products, reducing waste and pollution.
  • Textiles and Apparel: Hemp fabrics are durable, breathable, and biodegradable, making them a favorite for sustainable fashion brands.
  • Health Foods: Hemp seeds and oils are rich in omega fatty acids, protein, and essential nutrients, appealing to health-conscious consumers.
  • Paper and Packaging: Hemp’s quick growth cycle makes it a sustainable source for paper and biodegradable packaging materials.

Challenges in Scaling Hemp Industries

While hemp is making significant strides, challenges remain in fully integrating it into global markets:

  • Regulatory Barriers: Despite its benefits, hemp is still subject to regulatory hurdles in many regions, slowing its adoption.
  • Supply Chain Development: Infrastructure for processing and distributing hemp products is still catching up with demand.
  • Consumer Awareness: Many consumers remain unaware of hemp’s versatility and benefits, requiring ongoing education and advocacy.

Future Trends in Hemp Utilization

As innovation continues, hemp’s potential is far from being fully realized. Key trends to watch in 2025 include:

  • Hemp in Renewable Energy: Researchers are exploring hemp’s potential in biofuels and energy storage, offering exciting possibilities for a greener future.
  • Industrial Applications: Hemp fibers are being used in composites for automotive and aerospace industries, combining strength with sustainability.
  • Hemp-Based Pharmaceuticals: Advances in cannabinoid research are uncovering new medical applications for hemp-derived compounds.
  • Circular Economy Models: Hemp’s biodegradability and renewability make it ideal for circular economy initiatives, minimizing waste and maximizing resource efficiency.

Conclusion

Hemp’s growing prominence in 2025 reflects a broader shift toward sustainability and innovation. As industries and consumers embrace this remarkable plant, its applications will continue to expand, driving positive change across sectors. From the clothes we wear to the homes we build, hemp is proving that nature holds the key to a more sustainable future.

title.rendered: The Rise of Cannabis-Infused Beverages: A $10 Billion Market in the Making?

content.rendered:
Cannabis-infused beverages are quickly becoming one of the hottest trends in the cannabis industry. As we look to 2025, this rapidly growing market segment is expected to redefine how consumers engage with cannabis, blending convenience, discretion, and innovation. From THC-laden seltzers to CBD-infused teas, the drinkable cannabis market is on track to reach $10 billion globally, fueled by consumer demand for novel and healthier alternatives to traditional edibles and alcohol.

Why Cannabis Beverages Are Booming

Several factors are driving the explosive growth of cannabis-infused drinks:

  • Mainstream Appeal: Unlike smoking or vaping, drinking cannabis is socially acceptable and discreet, making it appealing to a wider audience, including those new to cannabis.
  • Precision Dosing: Advances in nanoemulsion technology allow for consistent and rapid absorption of cannabinoids, giving consumers a predictable and controlled experience.
  • Health and Wellness Trends: With many consumers moving away from alcohol, cannabis beverages offer a low-calorie, hangover-free alternative that aligns with wellness lifestyles.

Key Categories in Cannabis Beverages

The market is diversifying with products catering to a wide range of tastes and preferences. Popular categories include:

  • THC Seltzers: Carbonated beverages infused with THC provide an alcohol-free way to unwind, often mimicking the social experience of drinking beer or cocktails.
  • CBD Teas and Coffees: Offering calming or energizing effects, these drinks are perfect for consumers seeking a functional boost without intoxication.
  • Cannabis Cocktails: Premium mixes infused with cannabinoids are making waves in the luxury market, appealing to consumers looking for sophistication in their cannabis experience.
  • Wellness Shots: Small, concentrated drinks packed with CBD or other cannabinoids are marketed for specific benefits such as relaxation, sleep, or post-workout recovery.

Innovations in Cannabis Beverages

Technological advancements are key to the growth of this market. Some of the latest innovations include:

  • Nanoemulsion Technology: This process breaks cannabinoids into tiny particles that mix easily with water, ensuring fast onset times and consistent effects.
  • Customizable Experiences: Brands are experimenting with terpene profiles and cannabinoid ratios to deliver tailored effects, such as relaxation, focus, or euphoria.
  • Sustainable Packaging: Eco-friendly materials and designs are becoming a priority for brands seeking to attract environmentally conscious consumers.

Challenges Facing the Industry

Despite its promise, the cannabis beverage market faces several hurdles:

  • Regulatory Barriers: Navigating complex and varying cannabis laws across states and countries remains a significant challenge for manufacturers.
  • Shelf Stability: Ensuring that cannabinoids remain effective and palatable over time requires ongoing innovation in formulation and packaging.
  • Consumer Education: Many potential customers are still unfamiliar with how cannabis beverages work, making education a critical component of marketing strategies.

The Future of Cannabis Beverages

As the market matures, several trends are likely to shape its trajectory in 2025 and beyond:

  • Global Expansion: Countries with emerging cannabis industries, such as Germany and Thailand, are likely to embrace cannabis beverages as an entry point for new consumers.
  • Alcohol Partnerships: Collaborations between cannabis companies and alcohol giants could lead to more sophisticated and widely distributed products.
  • Functional Cannabis Drinks: The intersection of cannabis and health will likely produce more beverages targeting specific benefits, such as enhanced focus or stress relief.

Conclusion

Cannabis-infused beverages are more than just a trend; they represent a shift in how cannabis is consumed and integrated into everyday life. As technology advances and consumer preferences evolve, this market has the potential to become a cornerstone of the cannabis industry. For businesses and consumers alike, the next few years promise exciting developments that will redefine the possibilities of drinkable cannabis.

title.rendered: Cannabis and Mental Health: New Research on CBD’s Role in Treating Anxiety and Depression

content.rendered:
The relationship between cannabis and mental health has long been a topic of intrigue and debate. In 2025, however, new research is shedding light on how cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive compound in cannabis, is transforming the way we approach anxiety and depression treatments. With increasing societal acceptance and scientific exploration, CBD is emerging as a promising alternative or complement to traditional therapies for mental health.

Understanding CBD and Its Mechanisms

CBD interacts with the body’s endocannabinoid system (ECS), a complex network of receptors that helps regulate mood, stress, and emotional well-being. Unlike tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), CBD does not produce a “high,” making it more appealing for therapeutic use. Key mechanisms through which CBD influences mental health include:

  • Serotonin Modulation: CBD enhances serotonin signaling, which plays a crucial role in mood regulation and anxiety reduction.
  • Neuroprotection: Research indicates that CBD promotes neural regeneration in regions of the brain affected by chronic stress and depression.
  • Anti-Inflammatory Properties: Inflammation has been linked to depression and other mental health disorders. CBD’s anti-inflammatory effects may reduce these impacts.

Recent Research Highlights

New studies in 2025 have advanced our understanding of CBD’s potential for treating anxiety and depression:

  • Clinical Trials for Anxiety: A multi-site study published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research found that CBD significantly reduced symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in 75% of participants after eight weeks of treatment.
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD): Research from a leading medical university demonstrated that CBD, when combined with cognitive behavioral therapy, enhanced treatment outcomes for PTSD patients by improving sleep quality and reducing intrusive thoughts.
  • Treatment-Resistant Depression: In a groundbreaking trial, CBD was shown to provide relief for patients who did not respond to traditional antidepressants, opening new avenues for those struggling with treatment-resistant conditions.

Advantages of CBD Over Traditional Treatments

CBD offers several benefits that make it a compelling option for mental health treatment:

  • Fewer Side Effects: Unlike many pharmaceuticals, CBD has a favorable side effect profile, with fewer instances of fatigue, nausea, or dependency.
  • Rapid Onset: Some users report feeling the effects of CBD within minutes, making it a practical option for acute anxiety episodes.
  • Versatile Administration: CBD is available in various forms, including oils, capsules, gummies, and even beverages, allowing individuals to tailor their use to personal preferences.

Challenges and Considerations

Despite its potential, CBD is not without challenges:

  • Dosage Uncertainty: Optimal dosing for mental health conditions remains unclear, with efficacy varying widely among individuals.
  • Regulatory Hurdles: The lack of standardized regulations for CBD products raises concerns about quality and consistency.
  • Interactions with Medications: CBD may interact with other medications, underscoring the importance of consulting healthcare providers.

The Future of CBD in Mental Health

As research continues, several developments could further solidify CBD’s role in mental health care:

  • Personalized Medicine: Advances in genetic testing and AI could lead to personalized CBD treatments tailored to individual needs and biochemistry.
  • Combination Therapies: CBD’s integration with established treatments, such as antidepressants or psychotherapy, could enhance efficacy and patient outcomes.
  • Wider Acceptance: With growing public interest and ongoing advocacy, CBD is likely to gain broader acceptance as a legitimate mental health intervention.

Conclusion

CBD is transforming the landscape of mental health treatment, offering hope to millions who struggle with anxiety and depression. As we embrace the scientific advancements of 2025, CBD’s potential to alleviate suffering and improve quality of life represents a milestone in holistic and accessible mental health care. With further research and education, this remarkable compound could redefine how we approach mental well-being in the years to come.

title.rendered: Global Cannabis Policy Trends: Predictions for Legalization and Market Expansion in 2025

content.rendered:
The global cannabis industry has witnessed a seismic shift in the last decade, transitioning from a taboo topic to a burgeoning market with enormous economic potential. As we enter 2025, cannabis legalization and regulatory changes are poised to reshape global markets, influence international trade, and drive societal acceptance of this once-controversial plant. This blog explores key trends and predictions for cannabis policy and market expansion in the coming year.

The March Toward Global Legalization

More countries are moving toward cannabis legalization for both medical and recreational purposes. Some of the significant developments expected in 2025 include:

  • Europe’s Expanding Market: Germany’s recent move toward recreational cannabis legalization has set the tone for the European Union. Countries like France, Italy, and Spain are likely to follow suit, creating a unified cannabis market across the continent.
  • Latin America’s Progressive Policies: Uruguay and Mexico have led the charge in Latin America, and nations like Colombia and Argentina are expected to expand their cannabis programs in 2025, focusing on exports and domestic sales.
  • Africa’s Emerging Role: With countries like South Africa and Zimbabwe embracing cannabis cultivation for export, the African continent is becoming a key player in the global supply chain. 2025 could see more nations legalizing cannabis for medical use to tap into the economic benefits.

The Role of International Trade Agreements

As cannabis gains acceptance, international trade agreements are likely to incorporate cannabis exports and imports. Key developments to watch include:

  • Harmonization of Standards: Countries will need to establish standardized testing and labeling regulations to facilitate international trade.
  • Export Powerhouses: Canada, Israel, and Colombia are positioning themselves as leaders in cannabis exports, leveraging their advanced cultivation techniques and favorable climates.
  • Trade Barriers: Tariffs and restrictions could still pose challenges, especially in regions where cannabis remains federally illegal or stigmatized.

Shifting Societal Attitudes

Public perception of cannabis continues to evolve, with increased awareness of its medical and economic benefits. In 2025, we expect:

  • Normalization in Media and Culture: Cannabis products are becoming mainstream, with greater representation in advertising, entertainment, and everyday conversations.
  • Workplace Policies: As legalization spreads, businesses will need to navigate complex issues surrounding cannabis use and workplace safety.
  • Consumer Education: Governments and advocacy groups will focus on educating the public about responsible cannabis use, addressing misconceptions and safety concerns.

Economic Impact and Market Growth

The cannabis industry is projected to reach new heights in 2025, driven by increased legalization and innovation. Key economic trends include:

  • Job Creation: The cannabis sector is one of the fastest-growing industries, offering opportunities in cultivation, retail, technology, and research.
  • Investment Opportunities: Venture capital and institutional investors are pouring funds into cannabis startups, particularly in emerging markets like Africa and Southeast Asia.
  • Product Diversification: Beyond traditional flower and edibles, cannabis-infused beverages, wellness products, and pharmaceutical applications will continue to gain traction.

Challenges Ahead

Despite the optimism, challenges remain:

  • Federal vs. State Conflicts: In countries like the United States, federal prohibition continues to create a patchwork of regulations that complicates interstate commerce.
  • Banking and Finance: Access to banking services remains a hurdle for many cannabis businesses, hindering growth and innovation.
  • Regulatory Overload: Navigating complex and ever-changing regulations can be daunting for businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises.

Looking Ahead

As cannabis policies evolve, the industry is on the cusp of unprecedented growth and transformation. Governments, businesses, and consumers have a pivotal role to play in shaping the future of cannabis. With increased international collaboration, technological innovation, and societal acceptance, 2025 promises to be a landmark year for the global cannabis movement.

title.rendered: The Future of Hempcrete: How Hemp is Reshaping Sustainable Construction

content.rendered:
The construction industry is undergoing a green revolution, and at the forefront of this transformation is an ancient yet versatile material: hemp. With growing concerns about climate change, resource depletion, and the need for sustainable building practices, hempcrete—a bio-composite made from the woody core of the hemp plant mixed with lime and water—is emerging as a game-changing solution. As we move into 2025, the use of hempcrete is set to redefine how we think about building materials and sustainable construction.

What Makes Hempcrete Unique?

Hempcrete is not your average building material. It offers a combination of benefits that address critical challenges in the construction industry:

  • Carbon Sequestration: Hemp plants absorb significant amounts of CO2 during their growth, and this carbon remains locked in the hempcrete, making it a carbon-negative material.
  • Thermal Insulation: Hempcrete provides excellent thermal performance, reducing the need for energy-intensive heating and cooling systems.
  • Breathability: Unlike conventional concrete, hempcrete allows moisture to pass through, helping to prevent mold and improve indoor air quality.
  • Lightweight and Durable: While not as strong as concrete, hempcrete is lightweight and highly durable, making it ideal for non-load-bearing walls and insulation.
  • Sustainable Sourcing: Hemp requires minimal water, no pesticides, and grows quickly, making it an eco-friendly crop for large-scale use.

Innovations in Hempcrete Technology

As interest in hempcrete grows, so does innovation in its production and application. Here are some of the latest advancements:

  • Pre-Cast Hempcrete Panels: Companies are developing pre-cast hempcrete panels for faster and more efficient construction. These panels maintain the material’s eco-friendly properties while reducing on-site labor.
  • Enhanced Binding Agents: Researchers are improving lime-based binders to increase hempcrete’s structural integrity and longevity, broadening its range of applications.
  • Automated Mixing and Application: Innovations in machinery are streamlining the mixing and spraying processes, making hempcrete more accessible for large-scale projects.
  • Integration with Smart Technologies: Smart sensors embedded in hempcrete walls can monitor temperature, humidity, and structural health, offering data-driven insights for sustainable building management.

Hempcrete in Real-World Projects

Across the globe, hempcrete is finding its place in innovative construction projects. From eco-villages in Europe to sustainable housing developments in North America, the material is being embraced for its environmental and aesthetic qualities. In 2025, we’re likely to see:

  • Affordable Housing Solutions: Hempcrete’s cost-effectiveness and ease of use make it a viable option for addressing housing shortage

Optimizing Cultivation with AI

Companies are leveraging AI to identify and propagate cannabis strains with desired characteristics—whether it’s higher THC content, specific terpene profiles, or resilience to environmental stressors. title.rendered: Investment Surging in Marijuana Companies

content.rendered:

title.rendered: Swiss Study Further Validates Efficacy of the Cannabis Vaporizer

content.rendered:
It has long been known that vaporizing cannabis is an inherently healthier ingestion method than the traditional smoking of it, but it never hurts to have some published scientific research to back up the claims. Just over a week ago, a Swiss team of researchers published such findings in a scientific journal called PLOS One.

Using in vitro validation, which basically means doing your experiments in lab equipment and not in humans or animals, the four man team tested five different readily available cannabis vaporizers to determine if they could provide an accurate and effective dose of cannabinoids for the user.

 

 

The five vaporizer brands tested were:

  • Arizer Solo®
  • DaVinci Vaporizer®
  • Plenty Vaporizer®
  • Volcano Medic®
  • Vape-or-Smoke™

Using gas chromatography/mass spectrometry technology, similar to what is used in cannabis testing labs around the world, they were able to recover a certain amount of THC and CBD from the vapors, and then quantifiably measure those amounts to determine the efficacy of not only the five brands, but of vaporizers overall.

The study, titled Medicinal Cannabis: In Vitro Validation of Vaporizers for the Smoke-Free Inhalation of Cannabis, determined: “Temperature-controlled, electrically-driven vaporizers efficiently decarboxylate inactive acidic cannabinoids and reliably release their corresponding neutral, active cannabinoids. Thus, they offer a promising application mode for the safe and efficient administration of medicinal cannabis.”

As noted in the study, the reason that cannabis has been smoked for thousands of years to feel its effects is because the two main cannabinoids that we associate with being “high”, the THC and CBD, must be decarboxylated (or heated) in order to deliver those desired effects.

By igniting a bowl of cannabis flowers with a lighter, or even a hemp wick, the heat generated by the flame is much more intense than what is required for the decarboxylation process to occur.

As a result, the plant matter itself begins to combust creating carbon, tar, ash, etc.

The study concedes that the plant has been smoked for as many as 6000 years. So, if combusting that plant matter was a mainstream health concern, we’d probably have plenty of evidence by now to support it.

But, it is definitely true that certain respiratory illnesses or other medical constraints may make it so that smoking cannabis just is not an option for some users, and some just don’t like the flavor or effects of burnt cannabis.

So for folks like them, a study like this validates the use of a tabletop, or even an advanced handheld, vaporizer.

Full size vaporizer units like the Volcano Medic® have long given users the option to digitally dial in their exact temperature preference, and now even higher end handheld herbal and oil vape pens give users options via variable voltage batteries and digital temperature displays.

When set to around 400°F, a properly calibrated vaporizer should begin to decarb the full spectrum of cannabinoids and release the plants flavor and effects, without actually combusting any significant amount of plant material.

The full published study can be read here: http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0147286

It is fascinating to read about everything from the menial details (“Dried cannabis was grinded and homogenized carefully in a mortar and stored at 4°C), to the mindbending science and attention to detail applied to the research.

It’s also sort of amusing to see the sort of weed they have to work with over there, coming in at 4.61% THC. Eventually, studies like this won’t have to be limited to overseas labs with looser laws and maybe then we can see some true Cali OG Kush go through such an intense battery of scientific study.

Until then, we’ve strengthened the claim that vaping properly grown and harvested cannabis flowers is a legitimate and healthy alternative to smoking them..

by Dr. Brian C. Smith, the Sr. FTIR Product Specialist at PerkinElmer

title.rendered: BrainBot Looks to Take the Guesswork Out of the Cannabis Deal

content.rendered:
The BrainBot by PotBotics aims to neurologically link you to your ideal cannabis strain

A patient’s first time in a medical marijuana dispensary can be pretty overwhelming.

With the ink still drying on their freshly creased doctor’s recommendation, being buzzed back into a budroom often induces flashbacks to scenes from Willy Wonka & The Chocolate Factory – and yes, the Snozberry OG really does smell like Snozberries!

With some luck, there may be an honest, caring, and knowledgeable budtender on duty to help you make the right decision based on your needs…but, that’s exceedingly rare in the medical marijuana industry.

With thousands of different strains of cannabis on the market, any given dispensary may have 20, 30 or more options to choose from – each with its own potential medicinal effects.

Some of those effects can be highly beneficial. A strain that induces drowsiness, for example, would be good for an insomniac.

Those same effects, however, would not be so beneficial for someone who needed to walk into a business meeting an hour after imbibing.

So, knowing what ailments you are looking to alleviate with cannabis is the first step. Then, knowing which strain, or strains, will deliver the proper cannabinoid profile to acheive your goal is the next.

That is where cannabis tech pioneer David Goldstein, CEO of PotBotics, hopes to clear some of the smoke on the subject.

In a January 7th interview on MSNBC’s online-only program Code Forward, Goldstein took ten minutes to introduce a device that he believes will finally take the guesswork out of the cannabis deal.

At first glance, his new product, BrainBot, is fairly simple (and sort of silly) looking, but the technology held inside is the result of years of work in taking cabinet-sized hospital equipment, and reducing it down into a wearable headband.

BrainBot uses clinical EEG (electroencephalography) technology to map a medical marijuana patient’s neurological activity before and after smoking specific strains, to see exactly how different blends of cannabinoids affect them.

For the first time ever, says Goldstein, cannabis users have hard personalized data to reference, rather than the traditional “Yeah man, it feels good.”

As Goldstein points out, as long as cannabis remains a Schedule I drug on the federal level, the doctor who writes your recommendation for cannabis cannot and will not engage in a conversation about specific strains or even dosing.

BrainBot, Goldstein hopes, will fill that gap.

For example, the vast majority of new medical marijuana patients leave their doctor’s office with no idea that when we talk about cannabinoids, we are talking about THC – the psychoactive ingredient found in most marijuana that people associate with “getting high”.  Further, virtually none of them know that THC is just one of at least NINE medicinally beneficial cannabioids that can be found in the cannabis plant.

By educating patients about the effects of the various cannabinoids found in marijuana, they can then cross-reference detailed lab test results provided by their dispensary or caregiver with their own BrainBot profile to be sure that they are getting the medicine that works best for them.

 

BrainBot is a home-use 4-channel EEG device that uses state-of-the-art “dry” electrodes – meaning, they do not require any sort of lubricant or training for use. BrainBot is as simple to use as putting on a hat or a headband and lighting up some herbs.

Neural feedback is delivered via bluetooth to a nearby smartphone, tablet, or computer for future analysis by the user. That data can also be forwarded to a medical professional, potentially making a remote consult much more effective.

Goldstein sees real, practical medical solutions being achieved with his device. “Let’s say we’re talking about ADHD patients,” says Goldstein, “if they’re wearing an EEG and they’re trying medical cannabis usage, they could see when they stopped paying attention and by getting a prompt on their phone, on their computer, however it is they are using it, and they could refocus themselves. Those pathways in the brain can become stronger over time, with practice. So you’re looking at an age where brain-training will become possible.”

Will the BrainBot be a marijuana mind reader?

You can find out for yourself soon enough. BrainBot was featured at this year’s Consumer Electronics Show (CES), and should be available to the public by the summer of 2016. Goldstein says that a final retail price point has not yet been established, but that it will be “below the $300 mark”.

title.rendered: 3D Printing Takes Cannabis Packaging to the Next Level

content.rendered:
The idea of a functional 3D printer seemed like science fiction just a few short years ago, but like most technologies, it has evolved into a practical and affordable tool that anyone can now easily set up in the comfort of their own home.

Since 3D printing technology has gone mainstream, people have begun to churn out 3D-printed homes, handguns, and even 3D-printed 3D printer parts. So, it should really come as no surprise when some bored cannabis aficionados use their machine to start busting out custom printed bongs.

See a water pipe or rig that you like, but it is in a shop across the country? Simply purchase the schematics and download them directly to your own 3D printer and viola!

Whether or not that is what the future of headshops and smokeshops holds remains to be seen, but 3D printing technology is already being put to use in the cannabis industry – meeting a real need, instead of serving solely as a fad.

In Colorado, for example, with legalization came quite a bit of regulation and now all marijuana products – both medicinal and recreational – must be placed in a “childproof” container prior to sale.

The state’s clarification of the law reads: “Colorado has regulations for medical marijuana and now for retail marijuana. Colorado’s new Retail Marijuana Code covers three types of products: Marijuana, marijuana products including edible products, and marijuana concentrates. Before sale to a consumer, a retail marijuana store must place any of these products in a container that is child-resistant or place the container in an “exit package” that is child resistant. “Child resistant” packaging must conform to federal consumer product safety regulations and an ASTM standard; be opaque so the product cannot be seen; be closable if not intended for single use; and be properly labeled pursuant to the Retail Code.”

These specific packaging regulations put forth by the Colorado government led to a rush on repurposed medical-grade childproof packaging, but soon dispensaries might be able to print their own packaging in their very own office.

Green Technology Solutions (GTSO) is a cannabis-related business based out of San Jose, CA. They say that their goal is to help upcoming marijuana startups with business and technological support, and they have recently partnered up with a 3D printing firm by the name of 6th Dimension Technologies in hopes of changing the way that dispensaries package their pot.

GTSO and 6th Dimension have collaborated on a new line of 3D-printed locking childproof containers in a variety of sizes and styles that they hope to officially launch sometime in 2016.

“We’re working to engineer a rigid container that can be easily opened by an adult but remains inaccessible to small children,” GTSO CEO Wallace Brown told 420intel.com adding, “The prototypes that receive the best feedback from our focus groups will be patented.”

Some experts predict that the medical marijuana industry alone will be raking in over $5 Billion annually by 2018, and with full recreational legalization of cannabis on the 2016 ballot in California, ancillary companies who can help the main players stay in regulatory compliance will be very valuable.

Colorado has already been a lucrative market for such entrepreneurs, but there are more people just in west Los Angeles than there are in all of Colorado… so high tech/high efficiency solutions are about to be in high demand.

title.rendered: JAMA study confirms medical marijuana use associated with 24.8 percent decline in opioid overdose death rates

content.rendered:
The Jama Network reported that states allowing medical marijuana use saw a 25% decline in expected death rates from opiate use compared to states that have not legalized medical marijuana. This was reported in this article by the American Medical Association.

JAMA Internal Medicine

Official Results: States with medical marijuana laws had a 24.8 percent lower average annual opioid overdose death rate compared to states without such laws. In 2010, that translated to about 1,729 fewer deaths than expected. The years after implementation of medical marijuana laws also were associated with lower overdose death rates that generally got stronger over time: year 1 (-19.9 percent), year 2 (-25.2 percent), year 3 (-23.6 percent), year 4 (-20.2 percent), year 5 (-33.7 percent) and year 6 (-33.3 percent).

Bottom Line: States that implemented medical marijuana laws appear to have lower annual opioid analgesic overdoses death rates (both from prescription pain killers and illicit drugs such as heroin) than states without such laws although the reason why is not clear.

Author: Marcus A. Bachhuber, M.D., of the Philadelphia Veterans Affairs Medical Center, and colleagues.

Background: Prescriptions for opioid painkillers for chronic pain have increased in the United States and so have overdose deaths. However, less attention has been focused on how the availability of alternative nonopioid treatment, such as medical marijuana, may affect overdose rates.

Commentary: Legalization of Medical Marijuana and Incidence of Opioid Mortality

In a related commentary, Marie J. Hayes, Ph.D., of the University of Maine, Orno, and Mark S. Brown, M.D., of the Eastern Maine Medical Center, Bangor, write:  “If medical marijuana laws afford a protective effect, it is not clear why. If the decline in opioid analgesic-related overdose deaths is explained, as claimed by the authors, by increased access to medical marijuana as an adjuvant medication for patients taking prescription opioids, does this mean that marijuana provides improved pain control that decreases opioid dosing to safer levels?”

“The potential protective role of medical marijuana in opioid analgesic-associated mortality and its implication for public policy is a fruitful area for future work,” they conclude..

title.rendered: Following US Trends, More Canadian Teens Smoke Cannabis Than Tobacco

content.rendered:
The Ontario Student Drug Use and Health Survey has been held every two years since 1977 and serves as Canada’s longest-running scientific look at underage drug use.

The latest version, released on Wednesday by the esteemed Canadian Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), may have shocked some suburban Ontario hockey moms when they learned that 21% of the region’s middle and high school students have admitted to smoking weed in the past twelve months.

 

 

It should come as no surprise, however, to anyone who has paid attention to similar headlines coming out of the United States over the past few years. And also like here in the US, many of the more conservative headlines now coming from our neighbors in the north seem to be missing the point.

This latest Canadian study polled 10,426 Ontario students in grades 7 through 12 and found that as they got closer to college age, they tended to be more likely to have smoked some weed in the past year.  For example, 37% of grade 12 students admitted (keyword: admitted) to cannabis use, whereas the percentage for grade 7 students is listed only as “negligible” in this week’s report.

Again, looking at trends from America, this should come as a shock to nobody, as college-age cannabis use is also on the climb here in the States.

But still, the point lost in too many evaluations of these studies is that just 9% of those same kids surveyed said they had smoked a cigarette in the same past twelve months.

Kids are no dummies.
Cigarettes will kill them.
Weed will not.

The problem is, as Dr. Robert Mann, a CAMH senior scientist and one of the Canadian study’s co-authors pointed out in an interview with the Toronto Sun, “Currently, cannabis is illegal and you could get criminal record … (yet) it’s a drug that’s very commonly used.”

Instead of celebrating the drastic drops seen in teen tobacco use, too many anti-cannabis activists use these studies to focus in on the steady rise in teen marijuana use.

Cigarettes and tobacco products are sold in every corner and grocery store in Canada, yet kids grades 7-12 are deciding in droves against tobacco use, and that is great news!

Also lost in the debate are the disturbing statistics surrounding teen alcohol use and abuse.

Another legal product in Canada, endorsed by celebrities and professional athletes around the world, alcohol can and does kill Canadian teens every year.

Cannabis does not.

 

 

The CAMH study showed that a disgusting 18% of the 10,000+ students in Ontario admitted to having participated in “binge drinking” at some time in the past month! title.rendered: CBD Benefit Update – New Information on CBD’s Health Benefits

content.rendered:
CBD, or cannabidiol, is quickly changing the debate surrounding the use of marijuana as a medicine. CBD has been found very beneficial for humans and animals for a variety of health conditions and for health maintenance.

Patient surveys from September 2015 have this to say:

  • Medical marijuana patients are using CBD-rich cannabis for a wide variety of conditions, including serious and incurable diseases, and conditions that may respond poorly to FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. Over 12% are using it to address the side effects of cancer treatment.
  • Patients with psychiatric illnesses, mood disorders, neurological diseases and CNS injuries favor CBD-dominant cannabis medicines. Patients with pain and inflammation favor CBD-rich cannabis medicines with more equal levels of CBD and THC.
  • THC matters. Patients using the 4:1 CBD-to-THC were the most likely to report a reduction in pain or discomfort, and improvements in mood and energy. Patients using the 2:1 CBD-to-THC ratio reported the greatest improvement in overall wellbeing. This finding is consistent with scientific research indicating that CBD and THC interact synergistically to enhance one another’s therapeutic effect.
  • CBD-rich cannabis appears to be remarkably good at ameliorating pain (particularly in patients with fibromyalgia, headaches and migraines), and at improving patients’ sense of wellbeing, particularly for patients with PTSD.
  • Given that people using CBD-rich cannabis for “general well being” are the only group who reported a decreased feeling of well being and the most likely to report a worsening mood, it’s possible that CBD products may not be appropriate as a supplement for people who are otherwise healthy.

What is CBD?

Most people have heard of a chemical called THC, which is the ingredient in marijuana that gets users high. Attention is shifting to another compound in marijuana called CBD, for good reason. Some doctors are concerned about certain side effects of THC, but CBD doesn’t appear to present that problem, and evidence of CBD’s medical benefits continues to grow.

Here are five facts many people now agree on about CBD:

  1. CBD is a key ingredient in cannabis/marijuana

CBD is one of over 60 compounds found in cannabis that belong to a class of molecules called cannabinoids, believed to be healthy nutrients. Of these compounds, CBD and THC are usually present in the highest concentrations, and are therefore the most recognized and studied. CBD and THC levels tend to vary among different plants. Marijuana grown for recreational purposes often contains more THC than CBD. However, by using selective breeding techniques, cannabis breeders have managed to create varieties with high levels of CBD and next to zero levels of THC. These strains are rare but have become more popular in recent years.

  1. CBD is non-psychoactive

Unlike THC, CBD does not alter your mental state, yet may improve brain function. This gives the CBD chemical a significant advantage as a medicine, since health professionals prefer treatments with minimal side effects.

CBD is non-psychoactive because it does not act on the same pathways as THC. These pathways, called CB1 receptors, are highly concentrated in the brain and are responsible for the mind-altering effects of THC. A 2011 review published in Current Drug Safety concludes that CBD “does not interfere with several psychomotor and psychological functions.” The authors add that several studies suggest that CBD is “well tolerated and safe” even at high doses.

  1. CBD has a wide range of medical benefits

Although CBD and THC act on different pathways of the body, they seem to have many of the same medical benefits. According to a 2013 review published in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, studies have found CBD to possess the following medical properties:

Medical Properties of CBD Effects
Antiemetic Reduces nausea and vomiting
Anticonvulsant Suppresses seizure activity
Antipsychotic Combats psychosis disorders
Anti-inflammatory Combats inflammatory disorders
Anti-oxidant Combats neurodegenerative disorders
Anti-tumoral/Anti-cancer Combats tumor and cancer cells
Anxiolytic/Anti-depressant Combats anxiety and depression disorders

Unfortunately, most of this evidence comes from animals, since very few studies on CBD have been carried out in human patients. Removal of marijuana from the US Controlled Substance Act will open the door to widespread confirming US use studies in the US by health professionals.

A pharmaceutical version of CBD was recently developed by a drug company based in the UK. The company, GW Pharmaceuticals, is now funding clinical trials on CBD as a treatment for schizophrenia and certain types of epilepsy. Similarly, a team of researchers at the California Pacific Medical Center, led by Dr. Sean McAllister, has stated that they hope to begin trials on CBD as a breast cancer therapy. 

  1. CBD reduces the negative effects of THC

CBD seems to offer natural protection against the marijuana high. Numerous studies suggest that CBD acts to reduce the intoxicating effects of THC, such as memory impairment and paranoia. CBD also appears to counteract the sleep-inducing effects of THC, which may explain why some strains of cannabis are known to increase alertness.

Both CBD and THC have been found to present no to minimal risk of lethal overdose. However, to reduce potential side effects, medical users may be better off using cannabis with higher levels of CBD.

  1. CBD is still illegal unless sourced from legally imported industrial hemp

Even though CBD shows much promise as a medicine, it remains illegal in many parts of the world. CBD if extracted from US grown marijuana, is classified as a Schedule I drug in the United States and, until recently, a Schedule II drug in Canada. Canada has recently taken steps to decriminalize recreational marijuana throughout Canada.

Drugs and Patents Based on CBD

Despite this oppressive US regulatory environment as of November 2015, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recently approved a request to trial a pharmaceutical version of CBD in children with rare forms of epilepsy. The drug is made by GW Pharmaceuticals and is called Epidiolex. According to the company, the drug consists of “more than 98 percent CBD, trace quantities of some other cannabinoids, and zero THC.” GW Pharmaceuticals makes another cannabis-based drug called Sativex, which has been approved in over 24 countries for treating multiple sclerosis.

A patent awarded to the U.S. Health and Human Services in 2003 (US6630507) also covers the use of CBD as a treatment for various neurodegenerative and inflammatory disorders. There are dozens of issued and pending patents for synthetic versions of CBD, believed to be far less effective than naturally derived CBD therapy.

title.rendered: CBD Deemed Safe with Increasing Evidence of Medical and Nutritional Benefits

content.rendered:
CBD in marijuana does not get you “high.” The chemical in marijuana that causes the high (and many of its other effects) is delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC. But there are over 100 other cannabinoid chemicals in the plant; CBD is one of those. Different cannabinoids can have very different biological effects; CBD is not intoxicating (see Bergamaschi et al. 2011).

CBD first rose to public prominence two years ago as a result of a CNN piece on medical marijuana. However CBD’s potential as a therapeutic agent has been known since at least the 1970s in the US, when its anti-seizure properties were first examined in animal studies. A few clinical trials were also conducted in adults with epilepsy, some showing positive results.

Generating the renewed interest and excitement are the anecdotal reports published by CNN and other media giants that some children with otherwise untreatable severe epilepsies respond well to CBD extracts and oils (please see Porter & Jacobson 2013; Hussain et al. 2015). These developments were largely behind New York recently apporving medical marijauna. A followup to the CNN piece depicted the struggles of parents of children with a seizure condition called Dravet syndrome, who moved their families to Colorado in order to get CBD-rich marijuana legally. Several drug companies have recently developed CBD-based medications, and one of these, called Epidiolex, is now being tested in clinical trials. Epidiolex was developed by GW Pharmaceuticals and has been given to more than 400 children under the FDA’s expanded access (“compassionate use”) program. Drug companies have long known about the benefits of CBD and have filed many patents on synthetic versions likely less effective than the natural CBD extracts.

 

There is reason to believe CBD may have a range of uses in medicine, including in the treatment of seizures and other neurological disorders. In the impassioned, often emotional debates these days over medical marijuana, CBD is often cited as one of the main reasons restrictions on marijuana should be loosened.

A basic understanding of the way cannabinoids affect the body and the brain is helpful to making sense of some of the confusing and contradictory claims made by partisans on either side of those debates. Most cannabinoids (including THC) interact with specific targets on cells in the body, the CB1 and CB2 receptors. CB1 receptors are found mainly in the brain and are important for learning, coordination, sleep, pain, brain development, and other functions; CB2 receptors are found mostly in the immune system. The fact that chemicals in marijuana can speak the body’s chemical language (and cause both beneficial and harmful effects) is not surprising and does not make marijuana special. Many plants, including the opium poppy, tobacco, and coca are similar in that regard. Extracting and amplifying the medicinal benefits of such plants and minimizing their potential harms can lead the way to effective medications, but are also a major scientific challenge.

In marijuana’s case, future medicinal uses will most likely lie in drugs based on cannabinoid chemicals or extracts with defined concentrations that can be reliably produced. There are very few precedents for a whole plant being approved as a drug (only two “botanical drugs” are currently approved in the U.S.). This is because creating a standardized plant medicine poses major difficulties — especially in a case like marijuana where there are countless, widely varying strains and large numbers of chemical components about which little is yet known. Marijuana has over 500 chemicals in total, including the 100 or so cannabinoids, so we will still be learning about this plant for years to come. However, we are quickly learning a lot about THC and CBD, and because of its unique properties, CBD, especially, may be poised to make great inroads into our pharmacopoeia.

CBD has very little effect on CB1 and CB2 receptors (please see Pertwee et al. 2008). This is probably why it does not make people high and is not mind-altering; in fact, it may even blunt some of THC’s psychotropic effects. Most marijuana grown for recreational use is very low in CBD content (and high in THC). CBD’s actions in the body are not well understood, but they appear to involve several signaling systems besides the CB receptors, including a serotonin receptor.

title.rendered: Cannabis Business Taxation – IRC 280E – Olive v. Commissioner, 9th Circuit Court of Appeals Analysis

content.rendered:
Over $2 million in tax and penalties assessed San Francisco Vapor Room dispensary for not complying with federal income tax laws that apply to medical marijuana businesses – IRC 280E – Olive v. Commissioner, 9th Circuit Court of Appeals Confirming Deductibility of Cost of Goods Sold, but Denying Deductions of Ordinary or Necessary Trade or Business Expenses Connected to Medical Marijuana

Summary

On July 9, 2015 the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit confirmed the Tax Court decision of August 2, 2012 assessing deficiencies and penalties arising from taxpayer’s operation of a medical marijuana dispensary in California. The Circuit Court affirmed its earlier 2002 decision in DHL Corp. v Commissioner, that IRC 280E precludes deducting any amount of ordinary or necessary business expenses associated with taxpayer’s dispensary operations under federal law. While typically businesses are allowed to deduct ordinary or necessary business expenses under IRC section 162, IRC section 280E creates an exception to deductibility if the business is trafficking in controlled substances. Although the use and sale of medical marijuana are legal under California law, see Cal. Health & Safety Code sections 11362.5, the use and sale of marijuana remain prohibited under federal law, see 21 USC section 812 (c).

Discussion

The Tax Court in Olive v. Commissioner found the only income generating activity of the taxpayer Martin Olive, doing business as the Vapor Room, was the sale of medical marijuana. There was no charge for use of lounge services, for counseling services, provisioning vaporizers, providing food, yoga, movies or other amenities offered patients of the Vapor Room. Since the sole income producing activity of the Vapor Room was trafficking in a controlled substance under federal law, the courts concluded all expenses of operating the Vapor Room cannot be deducted for federal tax purposes.

Taxpayer argues its business consisted of caregiver services and selling marijuana. Because the taxpayers accounting system showed no revenue other than from selling marijuana, this argument was ignored by the courts.

The courts distinguished its earlier decision from 2007 in Californians Helping Alleviate Medical Problems (CHAMPS) v. Commissioner, where the taxpayer was found to be involved in more than one trade or business, with the primary one being extensive caregiver and counseling services. In CHAMPS the tax court concluded the primary purpose was providing caregiver services to its members. The court compared the Vapor Room to a bookstore that allows its guests to sit in comfortable chairs, drink coffee or team eat cookies, attend events, get advice, all for free while deciding whether to buy a book. The court explained CHAMPS however was like a bookstore that also sold coffee, pastries and food in a café like area, besides selling books.

The courts also stated that while Congress may not have intended 280E to apply to activities legal under state law, until Congress changes the statute it must be enforced based on its plain meaning as the courts have long done in a wide range of situations not foreseen by Congress when enacting tax legislation, as often occurs in tax interpretation cases. Finally the courts confirmed even if Congress decides not to expend funds to enforce federal law prohibiting trafficking in marijuana, has no impact on interpretation of tax statutes.

While the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals glossed over the issue of deductibility of cost of goods sold (COGS) even for marijuana dispensaries, the Tax Court in 2012 affirmed COGS are deductible and not subject to IRC section 280E’s prohibition of deducting ordinary or necessary trade or business expenses. The Vapor Room taxpayer however could not provide any receipts to support the COGS item on its tax returns, only its own ledgers. The court also concluded the testimony of the Vapor Room’s CPA was not reliable, and was not an adequate substitute for invoices or reliable documentation proving COGS expenditures. Nevertheless the court considered testimony on the average COGS of other dispensaries, and allowed a COGS deduction of 75% despite the IRS audit agent denying any COGS deduction.

Measuring COGS and explaining the expense items that may be included in it for marijuana businesses are beyond the scope of this article.

title.rendered: History of Marijuana and Cannabis Laws in the US

content.rendered:
The history of marijuana use and regulation in the US is indeed incredibly fascinating. Many of this country’s founding fathers and greatest patriots actually grew hemp as one of their farm’s main crops. They were literally “pot” farmers. It was not until many generations later in the 1900s that hemp/cannabis/marijuana became “bad plants” for reasons discussed in other articles you can find on Hempioneers.com.
  
Pre-Independence Days
  
When the Unites States was a young colony, England demanded payment of taxes by requiring some colonies to grow and export hemp. One could argue factually the first formal tax system in the colonies which became the United States of America required payment in marijuana.Regulation of Cannabis sativa began as early as 1619. The Virginia Company, by decree of King James I in 1619, ordered every colonist to grow 100 plants specifically for export. Thus, England’s only colony in America began to grow hemp in order to meet its tax obligation and to serve a growing demand for hemp in other British colonies.[2][3]
The 1st US president, George Washington apparently also grew hemp at Mount Vernon as one of his three primary crops. The use of hemp for rope and fabric was ubiquitous throughout the 18th and 19th centuries in the United States. Hemp may have been the US’s largest crop for many generations.
Medicinal preparations of cannabis became available in American pharmacies in the 1850s following an introduction to its use in Western medicine by William O’Shaughnessy a decade earlier in 1839.[4]

Cannabis fluid extract medicine bottle from 1906

The Puritanicallt Charged Unenlightened Days of the Early 1900s

Around the same time, efforts to regulate the sale of pharmaceuticals began, and laws were introduced on a state-to-state basis that created penalties for mislabeling drugs, adulterating them with undisclosed narcotics, and improper sale of those considered “poisons“. Poison laws generally either required labels on the packaging indicating the harmful effects of the drugs or prohibited sale outside of licensed pharmacies and without a doctor’s prescription. Those that required labeling often required the word “poison” if the drug was not issued by a pharmacy. Other regulations were prohibitions on the sale to minors, as well as restrictions on refills. Some pharmaceutical laws specifically enumerated the drugs that came under the effect of the regulations, while others didn’t — leaving the matter to medical experts. Those that did generally included references to cannabis, either under the category of “cannabis and its preparations” or “hemp and its preparations.”[5]

Increased restrictions and labeling of cannabis as a poison began in many states from 1906 onward, and outright prohibitions began in the 1920s. By the mid-1930s Cannabis was regulated as a drug in every state, including 35 states that adopted the Uniform State Narcotic Drug Act.[1]

Marihuana Tax Act of 1937

Prior to the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937, marijuana was widely used by medical doctors in the United States for a variety of physical and emotional ailments. The full text of the act can be read here. Extensive background on the act been be read here. It was not apparent in public debate at that time that the purpose of the act was to make marijauna illegal in the US, but it had that effect due to the nature of its enforcement provisions.

In the 1970s, many places in the United States started to abolish state laws and other local regulations that banned possession or sale of cannabis. The same thing happened with cannabis sold as medical cannabis in the 1990s.

All this is in conflict with federal laws; cannabis is a Schedule I drug according to the Controlled Substances Act of 1970, which classified cannabis as having high potential for abuse, no medical use, and not safe to use without medical supervision. Multiple efforts to reschedule cannabis under the Act have failed, and the United States Supreme Court has ruled in United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers’ Cooperative and Gonzales v. Raich that the federal government has a right to regulate and criminalize cannabis, even for medical purposes.

 

Controlled Substances Act of 1970 – The beginning of the Cannabis Medicine Prohibition

It was not until 1970 with passage of the Controlled Substances Act that marijauna became illegal federally for medical and recreational use.

Around this same time, the U.S. government began a litany of “reefer madness” propaganda and police actions that are with us today. Coupled with the bureaucratic demands of the tax act, the practice of physicians prescribing cannabis for therapeutic purposes in such an environment became subject to great scrutiny and therefore unwise. Cannabis’ therapeutic value was no longer taught in medical schools; it vanished from the pharmacopoeia of the U.S.; it became outlawed.

Many organizations today are focusing efforts  to re-institute cannabis as a legitimate medicine for use within the United States at the federal government level. title.rendered: Legal marijuana is the fastest-growing industry in the United States

content.rendered:
Legal marijuana is the fastest-growing industry in the United States. If the trend toward legalization spreads to all 50 states, marijuana could become larger than the organic food industry, according to a new report obtained by The Huffington Post.

“In the last year, the rise of the cannabis industry went from an interesting cocktail conversation to being taken seriously as the fastest growing industry in America,” Troy Dayton, CEO of The ArcView Group and publisher of the third edition of the State of Legal Marijuana Markets, said in the executive summary of the report. “At this point, it’s hard to imagine that any serious businessperson who is paying attention hasn’t spent some time thinking about the possibilities in this market.”

Over the next five years, the marijuana industry is expected to continue to grow, with ArcView predicting that 14 more states will legalize recreational marijuana and two more states will legalize medical marijuana. At least 10 states are already considering legalizing recreational marijuana in just the next two years through ballot measures or state legislatures.

To date, four states — Colorado, Washington, Alaska and Oregon — have legalized retail marijuana. Washington, D.C., voters also legalized recreational marijuana use, but sales currently remain banned. Twenty-three states have legalized medical cannabis. Still, marijuana remains illegal at the federal level.

The report projects that, by 2019, all of the state-legal marijuana markets combined will make for a potential overall market worth almost $11 billion annually.

title.rendered: Why Law Enforcement Agencies Oppose Legalized Marijuana – The Real Story

King, the study’s co-author and a research associate at the Sentencing Project. “Marijuana is the most widely used illegal substance … The question is, is this really where we want to be spending all our money?” King asks. This is only counting direct criminal justice system resource costs – the actual societal cost is likely ten times as great. Obviously there are many many public sector jobs in the law enforcement, courts and larger criminal justice system dependent upon continued criminal treatment of marijuana use.

title.rendered: Indiana’s First Church of Pot

content.rendered:
Be careful what you wish for: A ‘church of cannabis’ is the latest unintended consequence of the right’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act madness.
Hoosiers, get your Hookahs.In the latest Unintended Consequence of the “Religious Freedom” laws now sweeping the country, an Indiana church today was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS. But not just any church: The First Church of Cannabis, which proposes to exploit Indiana’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) to smoke pot at its services.According to Bill Levin, self described “Minister of Love and Grand Poobah” of the church, the first service is set for July 1, the day the Indiana RFRA takes effect. “We’re here for love, compassion, understanding, and good health,” Levin toldThe Daily Beast.  “We’re teaching what the original guys originally taught.”Despite the official IRS designation, it’s clear that the Church has a sense of humor. Posted on its Facebook page, the church’s core principles, “The Deity Dozen,” include “Don’t be an asshole” and “Do not be a ‘troll’ on the Internet.” And of course “Cannabis, the ‘healing plant’ is our sacrament.”

Since becoming an Internet sensation, Levin says the Deity Dozen has been translated into a dozen languages.

Alas, from a legal perspective, the First Church’s sense of humor hurts its chances of prevailing in court. Novel “churches” have been trying to use pot and other “sacraments” for decades now, and courts have had no trouble waving them away.

The question is whether RFRA changes the game. And the answer is no.

Underneath all the sound and fury, RFRAs like Indiana’s are actually very specific legal provisions. Technically speaking, what they do is increase the burden on the government to justify any law that impacts religious practice. Specifically, if a law “substantially burdens” the exercise of religion, the government must show that it has a “compelling state interest” and that the law is the “least restrictive means” to address it.
